items.stem: How is the issue of sustainability important for development? Explain with examples.
items.answer: Sustainability matters because development has to go on without exhausting the base it stands on. (1) Sustainable use of natural resources is the process by which economic, industrial and social needs are met while the resources are managed and exploited in such a way that biodiversity, the balance in the ecosystem and the biological cycles such as the carbon, nitrogen and water cycles are not destroyed. (2) Coal, oil and natural gas are chiefly used to provide electricity and to power vehicles; we should instead take advantage of the abundance of solar, wind, wave, tidal and thermal energy, which is free, renewable and sustainable, and which can supply enough green electricity for all our industries, homes and transport. (3) Sustainability lays emphasis on environmental protection and on checking environmental degradation, so as to stop over-exploitation and over-use of resources. Hence sustainability is important for development because it secures the resource base for the present without destroying it for the generations to come.

items.stem: Describe the importance of judicious use of resources.
items.answer: The importance of the judicious use of resources is as follows. (1) Resource planning: planning is an important step in a country like India where resources are enormously diverse; it provides an economically viable and sustainable solution to the issues related to resources and makes their use efficient and effective. (2) Management of resources: proper management is vital for the efficient and sustainable use of resources, as it successfully links human beings and resources and thereby results in their judicious use. (3) Awareness: awareness plays an important role in planning, management and use. It is the responsibility of every individual to plan and manage local resources affectionately and to harness them in the best and most sustainable way, for example by bringing a vacant piece of community land under use as a park or garden. Thus judicious use of resources keeps them available, productive and sustainable.

items.stem: Why is sustainability important for development? Explain.
items.answer: The issue of sustainability is important for development because: (1) with the passage of time generations change, and with that change society wants more and more benefits from the resources present in nature; (2) the needs of people keep increasing and things decay day by day, and excessive use makes matters worse — if the speed of use remains the same the available resources will soon be exhausted and the coming generation will be deprived of all kinds of needs; (3) growth and development should therefore be carried out keeping future usage in mind; (4) if resources are not sustained, our natural resources will be exhausted after some time and the upcoming generations will not be able to take advantage of them; (5) the concept stresses the role of the environment as capital. Sustainability is thus important because development that ignores it destroys its own resource base.

items.stem: How is the criterion used by the UNDP different from the World Bank for measuring the development of a country? Explain.
items.answer: The World Bank uses per capita income to measure development, whereas the UNDP (United Nations Development Programme) measures development on the basis of the Human Development Index. The Human Development Index is prepared on the basis of: (1) criteria that are among the most important for the development of a country; (2) the average age of a person in a country, which helps us know the health facilities of the country; (3) the education gained at three levels — primary, secondary and higher education; (4) the average income earned per person in a given area (city, region, country, etc.) in a specified year, calculated by dividing the area's total income by its total population, that is national income divided by population size. So the World Bank looks only at income, while the UNDP combines health, education and income.
items.ocr: The book expands UNDP as 'United Development Programme'; the standard expansion is United Nations Development Programme. The printed numbered list of HDI bases is loosely worded and has been cleaned up without adding new content.

items.stem: What are the main advantages of India's land under a variety of relief features?
items.answer: Land, on the basis of relief features, can broadly be categorised as mountains with very high to high altitudes, plateaus with moderate altitudes, and plains with lower altitude. In India about 30 per cent of the area is mountainous, 27 per cent is plateau and 43 per cent is plains, and each of these has specific advantages to be utilised. (1) Mountains are the source of many streams and rivers, some of them perennial; these regions have very high potential for hydro-electricity production and are also sites for eco-tourism. (2) Plateaus are mostly laden with minerals, fossil fuels and forests, and so are economically most productive. (3) Plains are the most important land resource for human beings; they are fertile, most of the food crops are grown there, and they are also exploited for the development of factories and roads. But all these advantages should be exploited sustainably.

items.stem:
Explain the classification of resources on the basis of origin.
or
Distinguish between biotic and abiotic resources.
items.answer:
On the basis of origin, resources are of two types: (a) biotic resources and (b) abiotic resources.
Biotic ResourcesAbiotic Resources
1.They consist of living things.They consist of non-living things.
2.They can continue to reproduce and regenerate their population in a favourable environment.They do not have the capacity to reproduce and regenerate their population.
3.They are renewable.They are non-renewable.
4.They are affected by the external environment.They are free from environmental effects.
5.Examples: crops, animals, birds, reptiles and fishes, etc.Examples: coal, petroleum, natural gas, iron-ore and aluminium, etc.

items.stem: How are potential resources different from stock resources?
items.answer: Potential resources are resources which are found in a region but have not been utilised because of a lack of capital or other reasons. For example, the western parts of India, particularly Rajasthan and Gujarat, have enormous potential for the development of wind and solar energy, but so far these have not been developed properly. Stock resources are the materials in the environment which have the potential to satisfy human needs but cannot be used because human beings do not have the appropriate technology to convert them into a usable form. For example, water (H₂O) is a compound of two inflammable gases, hydrogen and oxygen, but human beings do not have the required technology to use them as a source of energy. So the barrier to a potential resource is capital or development effort, while the barrier to a stock resource is technology.

items.stem:
Explain any four human activities which are mainly responsible for land degradation in India.
or
What are the reasons for land degradation?
items.answer: Some human activities such as deforestation, overgrazing, mining and quarrying have contributed significantly to land degradation. (1) Deforestation due to mining has caused severe land degradation. (2) Over-irrigation is also responsible for land degradation because it causes water logging. (3) Industrial effluents discharged as waste have become a major source of land degradation. (4) Mineral processing, such as the grinding of limestone for the ceramic industry, generates a huge quantity of dust that settles down on the land and degrades it. These four human activities are therefore the main causes of land degradation in India.

items.stem: “Alluvial soils provide food for more than half of the total population of India.” Give reasons in favour of this statement.
items.answer: (1) Alluvial soil is the most widely spread and important soil in India; it extends over the northern plains and also into Rajasthan and Gujarat through a narrow corridor. (2) It is also found in the southern part of India in the eastern coastal plains, particularly in the deltas of the Mahanadi, the Godavari, the Krishna and the Kaveri rivers. (3) Since these soils contain potash, phosphorus and lime in adequate quantity, they are ideal for the cultivation of crops like sugarcane, paddy, wheat and pulses. (4) Since they are highly fertile, the regions of these soils are intensively cultivated and densely populated. So it is true to say that alluvial soils provide food for more than half of the total population of India.

items.stem: How are resources classified into various types on the basis of their status of development? Give one example of each type.
items.answer: On the basis of the status of development resources can be classified into four types. (1) Potential resources: resources which are found in a region but have not been utilised, for example solar and wind energy in Rajasthan and Gujarat respectively. (2) Developed resources: resources which have been surveyed and whose quality and quantity have been determined for utilisation, for example coal, iron and manganese. (3) Stock: materials in the environment which have the potential to satisfy human needs but which human beings do not have the appropriate technology to access, for example geothermal energy. (4) Reserves: resources which can be put into use with the help of existing technical know-how but whose use has not been started, and which can be used for meeting future requirements, for example water in dams and forests. These four — potential, developed, stock and reserves — are the types based on the status of development.

items.stem: Distinguish between Bangar and Khadar soil.
items.answer:
Bangar SoilKhadar Soil
1.Bangar is the old alluvium. In other words, Bangar is older than Khadar.Khadar is the new alluvium. In other words, Khadar is younger in age.
2.Bangar often contains kankar nodules with calcium carbonates in the sub-soil.Khadar is finer, more sandy and free from kankar nodules.
3.Bangar is not renewed frequently. Hence, it is less fertile.Khadar is renewed frequently and is more fertile.
4.Bangar is found away from the river and higher than ground level.Khadar is found near river channels in deltas and in flood plains.

items.stem: Why resource management should be conceived as new conservation?
items.answer: (1) The term 'resource management' is now used in place of 'resource conservation'. Resource management emphasises the wise use of resources aimed at meeting current human needs without destroying the ecological balance and without jeopardising the needs of future generations; it thus involves policies or practices regarding how resources are allocated under given conditions for development. (2) Resource management should be conceived as the new dimension of conservation. The emphasis is upon flexibility and upon the minimisation of long-term environmental damage, while maximising net social welfare over time; it involves strategies of action that evolve tactics, methods and a variety of objectives. (3) It is becoming increasingly concerned with the protection and enhancement of environmental quality and with the establishment of new guidelines for the public use of common property such as air, water and landscape. Therefore resource management should be conceived as the new conservation.

items.stem: Describe the efforts made at the international level for the conservation of resources.
items.answer: The efforts made for the conservation of resources at the international level are as follows. (1) The Club of Rome advocated resource conservation for the first time in 1968. (2) In 1974 Gandhian philosophy was presented by Schumacher in his book 'Small is Beautiful'. (3) In 1987 the Brundtland Commission Report made a seminal contribution with respect to resource conservation; this report introduced the concept of 'Sustainable Development' and advocated it as a means of resource conservation, and it was later published as the book 'Our Common Future'. (4) In 1992 more than 100 heads of states met at Rio de Janeiro in Brazil for the first International Earth Summit to discuss the problem of environmental protection and socio-economic development; it adopted Agenda-21 for achieving sustainable development in the 21st century. These are the chief international efforts made for the conservation of resources.

items.stem:
Classify resources on the basis of ownership into four categories. Mention the main feature of each.
or
Distinguish between individual resources and community owned resources. Give any two differences.
items.answer: On the basis of ownership resources can be classified into four types. (1) Individual resources: these are owned privately by individuals, for example plots, houses, plantations, pasture lands and ponds owned by individuals. (2) Community owned resources: resources which are accessible to all the members of the community, for example grazing grounds, burial grounds, picnic spots and play grounds. (3) National resources: all the minerals, water resources, forests, wildlife and land within the political boundaries, and the oceanic area up to 12 nautical miles from the coast, belong to the nation. (4) International resources: the oceanic resources beyond 200 km of the Exclusive Economic Zone belong to international institutions. Thus ownership ranges from the individual, through the community and the nation, to international institutions.

items.stem: Why is it important to have a planned strategy for the development of resources in India?
items.answer: A planned strategy for the development of resources in India is needed for the following reasons. (1) In some resources India is very rich while in others it is very poor; proper planning will create a balance between the two and make the whole period of consumption and utilisation more scientific, rational and authentic. (2) The distribution of various resources in India is not the same region-wise or state-wise; regions having more resources can supply some of them to areas where resources are scarce or in less quantity. (3) Proper planning before use is very helpful in checking the misuse or destruction of valuable resources. (4) India can save its foreign currency through proper planning; for example, it can reduce the import of resources on which it depends entirely, such as petroleum products, which are available in very small quantity in India while their demand increases day by day. Hence a planned strategy is essential for the development of resources in India.

items.stem: For the development of any region, availability of resource is not enough, technology for proper exploitation of resource is also necessary. Justify.
items.answer: (1) More availability of resources, in the absence of corresponding changes in technology, hinders development. (2) In our country certain regions are rich in resources but economically backward because of the absence of technological development, for example the Chhattisgarh region. (3) Certain regions are poor in resources but economically developed because of developed technological know-how, for example Punjab. (4) Various countries of Asia and Africa were dominated by European powers primarily because those powers had a higher level of technological development. Therefore resources can contribute to development only when they are accompanied by appropriate technological development.
